title: Industrial Relations Code: unions, strikes and standing orders
author: Editorial Desk
summary: Trade union recognition, notice of strike and the 300-worker threshold.
body:
The **Industrial Relations Code, 2020** is the Labour Code that governs how workers organise, how unions and employers deal with each other, and how disputes, strikes, lay-offs and closures are handled. It is also the Code that has drawn the most debate among trade unions. This post sets out what it says, where it changed the older position, and what BMS and other unions have asked the Government to discuss.

## Background: three laws become one

The Code replaces three laws that have shaped Indian industrial life for decades: the **Trade Unions Act, 1926**, the **Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946** and the **Industrial Disputes Act, 1947**. The first gave unions legal recognition and protection. The second required employers to publish written conditions of service. The third created the machinery of conciliation, tribunals and labour courts, and set the rules on strikes, lay-offs and retrenchment.

According to the PRS Legislative Research summary, the Code was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 19 September 2020, passed there on 22 September and passed by the Rajya Sabha on 23 September 2020. The 2019 version of the Bill had been sent to a Standing Committee, and the 2020 text changed several numbers from that earlier draft.

## Trade union registration and recognition

The Code retains the registration of trade unions. A union must have as members at least 10 per cent of the workers in the establishment or 100 workers, whichever is lower, to be registered, according to PRS.

The new feature is the statutory recognition of a **negotiating union**. Where there are several registered unions, the union that has more than 51 per cent of the workers as members is recognised as the sole negotiating union with the employer. The 2019 Bill had set 75 per cent, and the figure came down in the 2020 text. Where no union reaches 51 per cent, the Code provides for a **negotiating council**, made of representatives of unions that have at least 20 per cent of the workers as members, with seats in proportion to their strength. The 2019 Bill used 10 per cent. Recognition lasts three years and can be extended by mutual agreement. PRS points out that the Code does not clearly say what happens when several unions have 10 per cent support but none reaches 20 per cent. This is a question the rules may need to address.

## Strikes and lock-outs

The Code requires **14 days' prior notice** of a strike or lock-out in all industrial establishments. Under the old Industrial Disputes Act, a notice period of this kind was compulsory only in public utility services. A notice is valid for 60 days. Strikes and lock-outs are barred while conciliation is pending and for seven days after it ends, and while a matter is before a tribunal or in arbitration and for 60 days after the award.

For workers and unions, this means that planning a strike now needs an eye on the calendar and on the status of any pending dispute. For employers, it applies the same notice discipline to lock-outs.

## Standing orders

Standing orders are the written rules of an establishment on classification of workers, shifts, attendance, leave and the grounds of termination. Under the Code they are mandatory for establishments with **300 or more workers**, up from 100 in the older law. The Code provides for a model set of standing orders and a process for certifying them. Employers say that a higher threshold removes paperwork for medium-sized units. Unions point out that workers in establishments below the threshold may have no written, enforceable service conditions at all.

## Lay-off, retrenchment and closure

For establishments with 300 or more workers, prior government permission is needed for lay-off, retrenchment and closure. Earlier the threshold was 100. PRS records that the Government can raise the threshold by notification, but under this text it cannot lower it. Other points include:

- retrenchment compensation of 15 days' wages for each year of service, together with preference in re-employment for retrenched workers;
- 60 days' notice for closure;
- a **worker re-skilling fund**, to which the employer contributes 15 days' wages of the retrenched worker, paid within 45 days of retrenchment according to one law-firm summary, so that the worker receives retraining support on top of retrenchment compensation.

## Fixed-term employment and dispute resolution

The Code recognises **fixed-term employment**, in which a worker is engaged by written contract for a set period. Such a worker is to get wages and benefits on par with permanent workers doing similar work, and becomes entitled to gratuity pro rata after one year of service. Expiry of the contract is not treated as retrenchment.

Establishments with 20 or more workers must have a grievance redressal committee. Disputes can be taken to conciliation officers, and then to a two-member industrial tribunal, with a National Industrial Tribunal for disputes of national importance. A dispute about an individual worker's dismissal, discharge or retrenchment is also treated as an industrial dispute, and PRS notes that the worker can go to the tribunal 45 days after applying for conciliation. Awards become enforceable after 30 days, though PRS flags that the Government can defer, modify or reject an award on stated public-interest grounds, which raises questions where the Government is itself a party.

## The debate

Employers argue that the higher thresholds and the recognition of fixed-term work give the flexibility that medium-sized businesses need to hire. Unions have a different concern. The thresholds decide how many establishments fall inside the law at all. The strike notice rule affects the ability to bargain from strength. The conditions on recognition decide which union sits at the table. BMS has said that these matters need re-examination, and has asked for them to be discussed in tripartite meetings, where Government, employers and unions sit together. In its pre-Budget letter of 6 January 2025, reported by Organiser, BMS asked for the anti-worker provisions in the Industrial Relations Code and the OSH Code to be removed, and for the remaining provisions to be notified. It also asked the Government to regularise contract workers.

## Why you should read the text

Headlines often squeeze a long Code into one line: "300 workers", "14 days' notice", "51 per cent". Each of those numbers sits inside a chain of definitions, exceptions and powers to change by notification. Anyone advising workers, whether a union office-bearer, an advocate or a labour officer, should read the Code and the rules made under it, and not rely on summaries. The same is true of this post.

## What remains to be done

The questions that matter next are practical. How will unions prove their membership for recognition? Will State Governments raise or keep the 300-worker threshold? How quickly will tribunals be set up and staffed? And will the tripartite consultation that unions have asked for take place before rules are finalised?

## A later update

The Ministry of Labour and Employment announced that the four Labour Codes would come into effect on 21 November 2025. A law-firm summary describes the Industrial Relations Code as being in force in full. Readers should check the notified Central and State Rules for the current position.
